conclusion.justification: The report concludes that probiotics do not reliably shorten acute infectious diarrhea, citing major Cochrane reviews and high-quality trials that found little to no effect, while acknowledging older or strain-specific meta-analyses suggested some benefit. This represents a cautiously unfavorable stance (leans_reject).
conclusion.label: leans_reject

report:
**Conclusion: not reliably.** The best available synthesis does **not** support a confident “yes” that probiotics shorten acute infectious diarrhea. The 2020 Cochrane review found probiotics probably made little or no difference in diarrhea persisting ≥48 hours, and it was **uncertain** whether they reduced overall duration. Its later plain-language update similarly says probiotics may not affect duration and that reliable further evidence is needed. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33295643/  
https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003048_do-probiotics-help-treat-acute-infectious-diarrhoea

Why earlier answers often said “yes”: older/smaller trials and some meta-analyses suggested an average reduction (one 2023 review reported about 23 hours shorter in children). But findings vary substantially by the exact organism/strain, product, dose, setting, and study quality—so results for one probiotic cannot be assumed to apply to “probiotics” generally. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1341321X23002775

Importantly, two large, high-quality 2018 pediatric emergency-department trials did not find better overall outcomes with either *Lactobacillus rhamnosus* GG or a combined probiotic versus placebo. https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1802598  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1802597

Thus, probiotics should not be relied on to shorten illness; oral rehydration remains central. Discuss use with a clinician for young children or medically vulnerable people.
